emergency.notes: Ecuador has a unified 911 emergency system in major cities. In rural areas and the Galápagos, response times may be significantly delayed. Tourist Police in Quito: (02) 254-3983.

travelAdvisory.summary: Exercise increased caution in Ecuador due to civil unrest, crime, and kidnapping. Some areas have greater risk. Ecuador has experienced significant security deterioration with gang-related violence, particularly in coastal areas and urban centers.

travelAdvisoryUK.summary: There is a high threat of violent crime in Ecuador, including robbery, express kidnapping, and carjacking. Take extra care in cities and be especially vigilant at night.

healthcare.costForTourists: Private clinics are affordable by Western standards. Clinic visit $30-80. Emergency room $100-500. Hospital stay $200-800/night at private hospitals. Public hospitals are free but overcrowded and have limited resources.
healthcare.pharmacyAccess: Pharmacies (farmacias) are widely available in cities. Many medications available OTC including some antibiotics. Pharmacists speak Spanish; limited English.
healthcare.hospitalNotes: Private hospitals in Quito and Guayaquil provide adequate care for most conditions. For serious conditions, medical evacuation to the US or Colombia may be necessary. Galápagos Islands have very limited medical facilities.
vaccinationsRecommended: Yellow Fever (required if arriving from certain countries; recommended for jungle areas)
healthcare.insuranceAdvice: Travel insurance with medical evacuation coverage is essential, especially for Galápagos travel. Altitude sickness is a concern in Quito (2,850m) — allow acclimatization time.
healthcare.summary: Ecuador has adequate private healthcare in Quito and Guayaquil, though facilities outside major cities are limited. The Galápagos Islands have only basic medical facilities, and serious conditions may require evacuation to the mainland or abroad.

vaccinations.name: Yellow Fever
vaccinations.note: Required if arriving from a yellow fever endemic country. Strongly recommended for travel to Amazon/jungle regions.

vaccinations.name: Hepatitis A
vaccinations.note: Recommended for all travelers due to food and water contamination risk.

vaccinations.name: Hepatitis B
vaccinations.note: Recommended for travelers who may have medical procedures or intimate contact.

vaccinations.name: Typhoid
vaccinations.note: Recommended for those eating outside major restaurants or visiting rural areas.

vaccinations.name: Rabies
vaccinations.note: Consider for jungle treks, rural areas, or extended stays.

vaccinations.name: Routine vaccinations
vaccinations.note: Ensure routine vaccinations (MMR, DPT, polio, flu) are up to date.

risks.name: Altitude sickness
risks.note: Quito sits at 2,850m. Allow 1-2 days to acclimatize before physical exertion.

risks.name: Malaria
risks.note: Risk in Amazon basin and coastal lowlands. Prophylaxis recommended for jungle travel.

risks.name: Dengue fever
risks.note: Present in lowland tropical areas. Use insect repellent and wear long sleeves.

risks.name: Traveler's diarrhea
risks.note: Common risk. Drink only bottled or purified water. Avoid raw vegetables and unpeeled fruit.

risks.name: Zika virus
risks.note: Present in lowland areas. Pregnant women should consult their doctor before travel.

controlledSubstances.note: Carry original prescription with doctor's letter. Keep in original packaging. Maximum 30-day supply.
Require original prescription. Keep in original packaging.
Cannabis is decriminalized for personal use (up to 10g) but remains illegal for tourists. Do not bring cannabis products into Ecuador.

medications.generalAdvice: Ecuador's customs regulations require prescription documentation for controlled medications. Carry medications in original packaging with a doctor's letter. Be aware that counterfeit medications exist in some pharmacies — use established chains.

scams.name: Express kidnapping
scams.description: Criminals force victims into a vehicle (sometimes a fake taxi), withdraw cash from ATMs, and release them hours later. Increasingly common in major cities.
scams.avoidance: Never hail street taxis. Use Cabify or Indriver (ride-hailing apps). Share your trip details with a friend. If forced into a vehicle, be compliant — safety first.

scams.name: ATM skimming
scams.description: Devices placed on ATMs capture card data and PINs. Criminals withdraw funds hours later.
scams.avoidance: Use ATMs inside banks or secure locations. Cover the keypad when entering PINs. Check for loose card readers before inserting your card. Use tap/contactless where possible.

scams.name: Fake police officers
scams.description: Men in plain clothes claim to be undercover police and ask to inspect your wallet for 'counterfeit currency.' They swap real bills for fakes or simply take your cash.
scams.avoidance: Real police check wallets at stations, not on streets. Demand to go to the nearest police station. Call the police hotline to verify officer identity.

connectivity.simOptions: SIM cards from Claro, Movistar, or CNT at airports and phone stores. Tourist packages ~$10-20 for 5-15GB. eSIM via Airalo. Coverage is good in cities but limited in Amazon and rural areas.
connectivity.wifiAvailability: Free WiFi in hotels, cafes, and restaurants. Patchy in rural areas and the Galápagos. Galápagos internet is expensive and slow.
connectivity.bestOption: Claro SIM for best national coverage. Buy at the airport on arrival.

cultural.tipping: Not expected but appreciated. Restaurants: 10-15% if service not included. Taxis: round up. Hotel porters: $1-2 per bag.
cultural.dressCode: Casual but modest. Cover up in churches. Highland indigenous communities appreciate respectful modest dress. Galápagos: practical outdoor clothing.
cultural.greetings: Handshake is standard. Women often greet with a cheek kiss. 'Buenos días/tardes/noches' (good morning/afternoon/evening) is expected.
taboos: Photography of indigenous people without asking permission
Disrespecting local customs in indigenous communities
Leaving trash in the Galápagos — strict environmental rules apply
Feeding or touching wildlife in the Galápagos
cultural.haggling: Expected at markets and craft stalls. Not practiced in restaurants or formal stores.

safety.lgbtSafety: Same-sex marriage was legalized in 2019 by court ruling. LGBTQ+ community exists in major cities. Exercise discretion in rural and conservative areas.
safety.soloFemaleSafety: Exercise caution. Street harassment (piropo) is common. Avoid walking alone at night. Use apps for transportation. Dress conservatively in smaller towns.
safety.notes: Ecuador has seen a significant increase in crime since 2022. Gang-related violence affects coastal cities. The Galápagos Islands are safe. Tourist areas in Quito's historic center and Cuenca are generally manageable with precautions. Avoid displaying valuable electronics. Do not hail street taxis.

practical.visaFreeCountries: US citizens: 90 days visa-free. UK, EU, and most Western nations: 90 days visa-free.
practical.bestTimeToVisit: June-September for highland trekking (dry season). December-May for coastal beaches and Galápagos (warm wet season). Galápagos: year-round, no bad time to visit.

immediate: Evacuate from designated hazard zones immediately when ordered by authorities
Wear an N95 mask or wet cloth over nose and mouth — volcanic ash causes respiratory damage
Protect water supply — cover containers as ash contaminates water
Stay indoors with windows and doors sealed to keep ash out
Do not drive through heavy ashfall — ash makes roads slippery and clogs air filters
after: Wait for official clearance from SGR (Secretaría de Gestión de Riesgos) before returning
Clean ash from roofs to prevent structural collapse
Do not allow ash to accumulate in water tanks
Follow IGEPN (volcano monitoring institute) updates for eruption status
resources: Secretaría de Gestión de Riesgos: www.gestionderiesgos.gob.ec

immediate: Drop, Cover, Hold On — get under a sturdy table or against an interior wall
Stay away from windows, heavy furniture, and exterior walls
If outdoors, move away from buildings, trees, and power lines
Do not run outside during shaking — most injuries happen when people run
after: Check for gas leaks — if you smell gas, leave immediately and do not use electricity
If on the coast, move inland immediately in case of tsunami
resources: Secretaría de Gestión de Riesgos: www.gestionderiesgos.gob.ec
